implementation_notes: On the JVM the classic form is a guard method whose body runs inside synchronized (AnyRef.synchronized 'executes the code in body with an exclusive lock on this'), with the state held in a @volatile field or an AtomicReference so other threads see the transition; the non-blocking attempts come from java.util.concurrent - ReentrantLock.tryLock, Semaphore.tryAcquire, BlockingQueue.offer - and AtomicReference.compareAndSet is often the whole pattern in idiomatic Scala (true means the transition was won, false means balk). Actor-style code usually serialises the state in a mailbox instead, which makes the guard non-racy by construction. Whenever shared mutable state is used, keep the predicate and the transition under the same lock.
pitfalls: A plain var without @volatile or an atomic reads a stale value outside synchronized, so a thread can balk forever on a state that already changed.
synchronized is reentrant on the JVM: a nested guarded call slips past a check meant to admit one caller and silently skips the intended work.
Inside actors (Pekko/Akka) the mailbox already serialises state; adding tryLock/CAS on top introduces a second concurrency mechanism and new interleavings.
